headline: Dry, warm Friday with highs in the 70s, then cooler with light rain Saturday and mostly dry weather into Monday.
summary:
A ridge, an area of high pressure that pushes the jet stream north, keeps western Washington dry and warm through Friday. Skies cleared this afternoon with temperatures in the mid to upper 60s. Friday should be a bit warmer, with highs in the mid to upper 70s and fairly dry afternoon air (relative humidity in the upper 30s to low 40s percent). Winds from the east will turn breezy tonight, strongest in the Cascades and nearby foothills, then ease by Friday morning.

The pattern changes over the weekend as a trough, a dip in the jet stream, returns. Winds will shift back to coming off the ocean on Friday afternoon. A weak front arrives Saturday with light rain: a few hundredths of an inch for most lowlands and about a quarter inch in the Cascades. Parts of central Puget Sound could get even less because of the rainshadow effect. Westerly winds will pick up Saturday afternoon and evening in the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet. Sunday will be cool and mostly dry, with highs in the upper 50s and low 60s.

The summary at the top mentions more rain early next week. The detailed discussion says most computer models track Monday's low-pressure system south of western Washington, which would keep Monday dry but cool. Another weak front could bring isolated showers Wednesday into Thursday, but it does not look particularly strong.

timeline.what: Breezy east winds, strongest in the Cascades and foothills with gusts likely 25-30 mph, easing by Friday morning. Fog should be limited, though isolated patchy fog is possible in the south Sound and fog-prone valleys.
Dry and slightly warmer, with highs in the mid to upper 70s and afternoon humidity dipping to the upper 30s to low 40s percent. Winds turn onshore (off the ocean) in the afternoon.

A weak front brings light rain: a few hundredths of an inch for most lowlands and about a quarter inch in the Cascades. Central Puget Sound may see less. Westerly winds rise in the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet in the afternoon and evening.
Cool and mostly dry, with highs in the upper 50s and low 60s.
Most model guidance keeps a low-pressure system south of the area, so it should stay dry but cool.
A weak front from a low over the Gulf of Alaska may arrive and could bring isolated showers through Thursday. It does not look particularly strong.

confidence: Forecasters are fairly confident in the dry, warm Friday and the light rain on Saturday. Fog Friday morning is less certain: it is expected to be limited, but isolated patches may still form. Monday is less certain because the forecast depends on most, not all, models keeping the low-pressure system south of the area. The midweek front is expected to be weak, with only isolated showers possible.

glossary.definition: An area of high pressure in the upper atmosphere that usually brings dry, settled, warmer weather.
A dip in the jet stream that usually brings cooler air and a better chance of clouds and rain.
Wind blowing from land toward the ocean, which in western Washington means air from the east. It tends to dry things out and can limit fog.
Wind blowing from the ocean toward land. It brings cooler, moister air to western Washington.
The boundary between two different air masses. Fronts often bring clouds, rain, and shifting winds.
Receiving less rain because nearby mountains or terrain block or weaken the moisture. In this forecast it refers to parts of central Puget Sound.
A dip in the jet stream, with low pressure, over the northeast Pacific. It can send weak weather systems toward Washington.
